clips.text: Today trains your ear, not your mouth. Real Mexican Spanish, spoken fast among people who know each other, drops sounds constantly — and you already own most of the sentences underneath it.
So say nothing for the next few minutes. The exercise today is entirely your ears.
Ten at night, a busy taco stand. Two regulars order past you, back to back, and neither sentence slows down for a visitor.
¿Me da dos de pastor y uno de bistec, pa' llevar?
Va, ahorita se los preparo.
You didn't catch that, and your ear is fine. Every pattern in it is one you're about to meet slowed down first.
First pattern, and the most common: está shrinks to 'tá. Here it is in full, the way you learned it.
¿Dónde está el baño?
¿Dónde 'tá el baño?
Second: para shrinks to pa'. You already asked this exact question in part seventeen, at the pharmacy counter.
¿Necesito receta para este medicamento?
¿Necesito receta pa' este medicamento?
Third: nada shrinks to na'. This one you said at a restaurant table, about a peanut allergy — it matters more than most.
No puedo comer nada que contenga cacahuate.
No puedo comer na' que contenga cacahuate.
Fourth, and this one you'll hear constantly: pues shrinks to pos, or even just pus. It's a filler word, a small verbal shrug.
Pues no sé, tú dime.
Pos no sé, tú dime.
One more, and it's not a missing letter but a missing letter's cousin: the d between two vowels in -ado endings often just disappears. Cansado becomes cansao. Ocupado becomes ocupao.
None of these four patterns are mistakes, and none are regional oddities — they're what relaxed, everyday Mexican Spanish actually sounds like, everywhere in the country.

On top of that, the accent itself shifts by region: central Mexico tends to run fast and clipped, the coast has more of a sing-song lift, the Yucatán carries a Maya-influenced rhythm, and the north has its own distinctive pull. We won't fake demonstrating each one for you — that takes a real ear from each place, not a course. Just expect variety, not one single 'Mexican accent.'
Now, back to the taco stand. Same two sentences you heard at the start — listen again with all four patterns in your ears.
You got it. Nothing new went into your head today — what changed is that you can find your own sentences with pieces missing.

A01 complete. Está to 'tá, para to pa', nada to na', pues to pos — four small erosions, and underneath every one of them is a sentence you already built. Count the beats, not the letters, and keep going.
Listen to two regulars ordering fast at a taco stand, then answer about what you heard.
¿Me da dos de pastor y uno de bistec, pa' llevar?
Va, ahorita se los preparo.
